steps: Plan the location & permit
Check permits and requirements with the local authority having jurisdiction. Pick a spot that avoids cutting floor and roof joists, and plan fireplace, chimney and options together before starting.

No special floor reinforcement is needed. Run the chimney up inside the house if possible; an outside chimney should be in an insulated enclosure, since a cold chimney causes poor draft.

Many options need wiring or electricity: run it during framing if they may ever be added. The framing examples (Figure 6) are a dimensioned diagram on this page for the louvered unit, drawn larger than required; the Heat Dump option needs an extra 12" on its side.

RSF strongly recommends installation and service by professionals certified by the National Fireplace Institute (U.S.) or Wood Energy Technology Transfer Inc. (Canada).
Fit the top standoff

Before installing the fireplace, make sure the back shield is open on the back side (Figure 9), then fasten the supplied standoff to the top with the screws in the manual bag. Never fill the gap between fireplace and standoff; the finishing material covers it.
Anchor to the floor

The fireplace must be attached to the floor: reuse the four small crate brackets around the casing or base, placed as they were on the crate, with at least one screwed into a floor joist with 2" wood screws if possible.
Frame the enclosure

Any suitable material (2x4 or 2x6 studs, plywood, gypsum board), but no combustibles closer than the standoffs, top, back and sides, and none directly above the unit except framing for the facing and mantel. Hold the Table 1 (C) ceiling height: 7' sealed, 6' vented.

A vented enclosure needs regular 3"x10" or larger grilles in holes cut within 1' of both the floor and the ceiling (vertical or horizontal). The area above the fireplace stays free of combustibles up to the Table 1 (C) height, and the ceiling firestop is never closer to the fireplace base than that. Never pack required air spaces with insulation or other materials.
Connect the outside air duct

Insulated aluminium flexible duct rated over 200° F, from the outside inlet to the fireplace sleeve: 4" if the total run is under 25', 5" for longer runs. Max 12' vertical rise above the unit base; the inlet sits at least 5' below the rain cap and never in an attic.

1. Cut a 4 ¼" hole in the outside wall (5 ¼" for 5" duct), push the inlet in from outside and seal the joint.
  2. At each end, pull back the insulation and plastic cover and screw the duct to the inlet and to the fireplace sleeve with metal screws.
  3. Push the insulation and cover back and tape the cover with 2" aluminium duct tape.

Both 4" and 5" sleeves are supplied. Looping the duct makes a cold air trap. Don't crimp it at corners.
Run the EXCEL chimney

7" ICC EXCEL only, at least 2" from combustibles with no insulation in that space. Frame 13" square openings (up to 13 ½", never smaller), fit a radiation shield at every floor and a shield plus storm collar in the attic.

Remove the flue adapter, screw it to the first chimney length, then refit it to the fireplace with the original screws. Follow the EXCEL manual for supports, bracing and anchors.

Offsets

An elbow may sit directly on the fireplace. Max offset angle 30° in the USA, 45° in Canada; max four elbows (two offsets and returns). Fasten every joint with 3 metal screws and add a wall or offset support above each offset. A through-wall offset needs an angled wall insulated radiation shield (XM-7EWRSI30 or XM-7EWRSI45).

Masonry chimney

EXCEL runs from the fireplace to a listed liner (EXCEL, or ULC-S635, ULC-S640 or UL-1777) fitted inside the clay liner to the top. Join them with the FO-FDM7 masonry adaptor (3 rivets, 3 screws), install at least one 18" EXCEL length after the elbow, and keep the entry at least 12" from the ceiling. An existing chimney must first be inspected by the authority having jurisdiction.
Roof, flashing & cap

Extend at least 3' above the roof contact point and 2' higher than any wall, roof or building within 10'; brace it if it stands more than 5' above the roof. Fit roof radiation shield XM-7ERRS 1" above the roof line, then flashing, storm collar and rain cap.

• Vented flashing if the chimney is enclosed to the roof; regular flashing if it isn't.
  • Seal the flashing with roofing tar (under the upper shingles, over the lower) and nail it.
  • Seal the storm collar to the chimney with silicone, not roofing tar.
  • Secure the rain cap tightly.

For an outside chimney, RSF recommends a chase built as an extension of the home: insulate to at least the first firestop in a mild climate, to the top in a very cold one, and insulate the chase ceiling.
Finish the facing

Facing must be non-combustible (brick, slate, ceramic tile); gypsum board is not acceptable and stays outside the side standoffs and the 39 ¼" top clearance. Covering the top louver requires the supplied Louver Blocking Plate and two gravity vent kits.

Thin materials such as ceramic tile or sliced brick can go on with the rock retainer kit (FO-KK) or directly on the face with high temperature silicone. Without the top louver, two gravity vent kits are mandatory; leaving them out overheats the unit. Use only genuine RSF parts.
Hearth extension & spark guard

Non-combustible hearth at least 18" deep and 42" wide, centered on the opening; no minimum thickness. On a combustible floor, center the supplied 5" x 36" spark guard half under the fireplace (2½" beneath it) and half under the hearth.
Not needed on a non-combustible floor. A raised installation needs a custom guard (not supplied): Z-shaped for a gap of 2 ½" or less, right-angle above 2 ½". Details are in the Hearth extension spec.
Mantel
Set any combustible shelf per Table 2: 32" to 36 ½" above the opening for 0" to 12" depth. Side posts must be non-combustible unless they meet the 16" side-wall clearance.

panels.title: Smoke spills into the room
items: Door opened too quickly → open it more slowly
Dirty chimney or plugged cap (screened caps clog with creosote)
Chimney too short → Table 3, allowing for altitude and elbows
Central heat or internal blower running → turn it off before opening
Range hood or bath fan lowering house pressure → open a nearby window a little
Too little kindling → fire not hot fast enough at lighting

panels.title: Burns excessively fast
items: Air leaking past door seals or gaskets → paper test; replace gaskets (door can't be tightened)
Excessive draft → hotter fire, shorter burns, less heat recovery
Large amounts of paper, cardboard, mill ends or construction waste → over-fire

panels.title: Catalyst not giving heat
items: Bypass closed before the fire was hot → catalyst dirties, no extra heat
Ash on the catalyst face → soft brush and vacuum when cold
No red glow in a hot fire with the bypass closed → not firing
Not firing for several days, even in a hot fire → replace (FO-CATP)

panels.title: Weak draft
items: Smoke in the room, hard to light → add chimney height (most common fix)
Often wrongly blamed on a blocked air intake
Cold outside chimney → insulated chase enclosure
Severely depressurized house → outside air won't stop the smoking

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
1. Pull the bypass handle all the way out (bypass open). Leave it out until the fire is hot, about 15-30 minutes.
  2. Open the air control lever, on the right below the door, all the way to the right.
  3. Lay crumpled newspaper (5-6 pieces should do) and crisscross plenty of kindling over it. Never use flammable liquids.
  4. Light the paper and close the door most of the way, but not completely.
  5. When the kindling burns steadily, add at least 3 small pieces of seasoned wood, using the andirons so you don't smother the fire.
  6. Once the wood is lit, close the door completely. If the fire goes out, you closed it too early.
  7. When the fire is hot, push the bypass handle in to engage the catalyst.
Note: p. 11 (and p. 4, p. 28) says the air control lever is open when it's all the way to the right; p. 9 says it's all the way open when it's up.
Note: p. 11 says to leave the door slightly open while lighting, until the wood is lit; p. 3 says to operate the fireplace with the door fully closed, and warns that a partly open door can draw gas and flame out.

Your first few fires

Expect a slow start. The firebricks hold moisture from manufacturing and look black until a few hot fires dry them; then they turn white. No small break-in fires are needed. A slight odor from curing paint and oil can set off your smoke detector, so open doors and windows.

catalyst.title: The bypass and the catalyst
catalyst.html:
The catalyst burns off smoke, so you get more heat and a cleaner burn. The bypass handle decides whether smoke goes through it.

Handle pulled all the way outBypass open: lighting and reloading
Handle pushed all the way inCatalyst engaged: once the fire is hot

Push it in only when the fireplace is hot, typically after 15 to 30 minutes. Engaged too early, the catalyst gets dirty and gives no extra heat. Two temperatures matter. The smoke passing through the catalyst must be at least 150°C-300°F, or soot builds up on it, cutting performance and adding maintenance (p. 4). The catalyst itself must reach at least 175°C (350°F) before it starts burning off smoke.

Reading the catalyst temperature

A built-in probe reads within 1" of the catalyst. Connect the optional Digital Temperature Display (FO-DTD) or any standard Type K thermocouple thermometer; the wire is on the left side, inside the casing. Read it with the bypass closed.

Below 175°C (350°F)Add wood, open the air, keep the bypass open
175°C (350°F) to 700°C (1300°F)Just right: bypass closed except to reload
Above 700°C (1300°F)No more wood; close the air and let it die down

Every overheat shortens the catalyst's life.

air.title: Controlling the burn
air.html:
The door seals the firebox, so all combustion air comes in through the air control lever on the right, below the door. More air makes a faster, hotter fire; less air slows it and extends the burn time.

Note: p. 9 says the air control lever is all the way open when it's up; p. 4, p. 11 and p. 28 say it's open when it's all the way to the right.

Finding the right setting

For the first few days, run with the control fully open. Then close it in steps and watch the fire. If it smolders with no visible flames, give it more air. If nothing changes, keep closing, eventually all or most of the way. You should always see flames in the firebox.

The automatic damper

A bi-metal coil lets in more air when the fireplace is cold and less when it's hot, so it doesn't overheat. Once it's hot, small lever moves do more. Use the lever as your main control, and never tamper with the factory-set air control. The optional thermostat kit (FO-FDHC4) runs the draft control from a wall thermostat.

Outside or room air

A sliding door behind the bottom louver, below the firebox, picks the air source: push it toward the back for outside air, or pull it toward the front for room air. Colder outside air helps start the fire.

reload.title: Reloading the fire
reload.html:
Have your next load ready before you open the door: the catalyst cools fast while it's open. But don't rush.

  1. Pull the bypass handle all the way out.
  2. Turn off the central heat and internal blowers, if you have them. Running blowers can push smoke out.
  3. Open the door slowly.
  4. Poke and stir the leftover wood, then add the new logs. Keep a clear path in front of the pilot, the metal tube between the two andiron posts that feeds air to the coals.
  5. Leave the door slightly ajar for about 3-10 minutes, until the new wood is well lit, then close it.
  6. Push the bypass handle back in.
Note: p. 12 says to keep the door slightly ajar after loading, until the new wood is well lit; p. 3 says to operate the fireplace with the door fully closed, and warns that a partly open door can draw gas and flame out.

If smoke comes into the room

  • Open the door more slowly.
  • Shut off kitchen range hoods and bathroom fans; they affect the pressure in the house.
  • Open a window near the fireplace a little until the draft is established.
  • Make sure the chimney is clean and the cap isn't plugged.
  • When lighting, use enough kindling to get a hot fire quickly.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn seasoned cordwood: cut, split and dried under cover for at least 6 months, preferably a year or more. Dry seasoned wood is generally under 20% moisture. Densified fuel logs, alone or mixed with wood, are also fine.

Wet wood is hard to burn, gives little heat, builds creosote and darkens the glass. Hardwoods burn longer and more evenly, because more weight fits in the firebox.

Never burn

  • Driftwood, treated wood, coal, garbage or plastic
  • Chemical chimney cleaners, which ruin the catalyst
  • Construction scraps as your only fuel; they can overheat and seriously damage the fireplace
  • Large amounts of paper, cardboard or mill ends, which can over-fire it or start a chimney fire in a dirty flue

Wax fire logs

Not recommended, because they dirty the glass. If you use them, burn only one at a time and don't poke or stir it. Use only fire logs evaluated for fireplace use, and read the package warnings first.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
With controlled combustion, the fire isn't always hot enough to keep the glass perfectly clean. A good hot fire once a day usually burns off most deposits. The drier the wood and the hotter the fire, the cleaner the glass.

When you do clean it

  • Wait until the glass is cool. Cleaning it hot can cause a serious burn.
  • Use a cleaner your dealer recommends. Wood stove glass cleaners work far better than regular glass or oven cleaners. Never use an abrasive cleaner.
  • Heat won't break the glass, but impact can. Don't hit it, and don't slam the door.
Keep glass cleaner off the paint. It can remove the finish and make touch-ups difficult.

The rest of the finish

Wipe the painted and plated parts with a soft damp cloth, mild detergent and water, never abrasives. Touch up the face with Stove Bright Metallic Black high temperature paint, only when the fireplace is cool and the room is well ventilated.

chimney.title: Chimney, creosote and ashes
chimney.html:
Slow fires make tar and vapors that condense in the cool chimney as creosote. If it ignites, it makes an extremely hot fire.

  • Check the chimney about every week until you learn how often it needs cleaning.
  • Clean it once soot or creosote reaches 1/8" (3mm).
  • Soot or creosote more than 1/8" (3mm) thick means the chimney needs cleaning immediately (p. 4). That may also mean changing how you burn and checking more often.
  • To sweep, close the door, open the bypass and use a 7" round brush. Then vacuum any creosote or ash that fell into the top of the fireplace, through the bypass opening, with a flexible attachment.
  • Never burn chemical chimney cleaners. They ruin the catalyst.

Ashes

Remove ashes before they get deep enough to spill when you open the door. Put them in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid, and set it on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything combustible. Keep them in the closed container until all cinders are thoroughly cool. The optional Ash Pan Kit (FO-AP) lets you sweep ashes through a hole into a pan you empty from the bottom louver.

care.title: Catalyst, door seal and firebrick care
care.html:
Catalyst

Look at the catalyst at least three times each heating season. If ash is stuck to its face, clean it when it's cold: brush gently with a soft bristle brush, such as a paint brush, and vacuum near the face without touching it. Never use scrapers or hard brushes, and don't try to clean the individual openings.

Getting less heat than before? In a hot fire with the bypass closed, the catalyst should glow red. If it doesn't fire for several days, even in a hot fire, it needs replacing. It lasts about 5-10 years; your RSF retailer sells the Catalyst Replacement Kit (FO-CATP).

Door seal

Latch the door on a thin sheet of paper and pull gently but firmly. If it tears or is hard to pull out, the seal is good. Check all sides. The door can't be adjusted tighter, so replace worn gaskets with a kit from your RSF dealer. A leaky door wastes wood, can over-fire the fireplace and wears out the catalyst early.

Firebricks

Small cracks and wear are fine. Replace bricks only when pieces are missing or you can see the firebox metal through them.

safety.title: Safety and overfiring
safety.html:
• Keep furniture, firewood and other combustibles at least 4' from the front of the fireplace.
  • Have at least one smoke detector on each level of the house and at least one carbon monoxide detector.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire, and keep them well away while it's in use.
  • Don't use a grate or raise the fire. Keep it behind the andirons, and move logs that fall against the glass.
  • Don't slam the door; the glass can break.
  • Don't run it with the catalyst removed or deactivated, or tamper with the factory-set air control. Both are against federal regulations.
  • Don't install an insert, a gas log lighter or an unvented gas log set.
Don't overfire it. You're overfiring if you can't slow the fire down, or if the chimney connector behind the top louver glows red. Damage from over-firing isn't covered by the warranty.

RSF strongly recommends installation and service by professionals certified by the National Fireplace Institute in the U.S. or by Wood Energy Technology Transfer Inc. in Canada.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
RSF warrants its wood-burning fireplaces against defects in material and workmanship for 30 years, on a sliding scale:

First yearDefective parts repaired or replaced, plus reasonable labor
Second through fifth yearsParts repaired or replaced; no labor
Sixth through thirtieth yearsReplacement parts, if available, at 50% of published retail; no labor
Electrical componentsOne year only
Catalytic combustor5 years from original retail purchase

On a catalyst claim you pay a share of the then-current retail price: nothing for the first 2 years, then 60% in the 3rd year, 70% in the 4th and 80% in the 5th. Return it to your dealer with a Combustor Failure Report (on the RSF website) and your original proof of purchase.

Not covered

  • Glass and plating
  • Normal wear: paint discoloration, worn gaskets, eroded or cracked refractory
  • Vandalism, neglect, abuse, over-firing, improper fuel or fuel loads, or skipped servicing
  • Installations that don't follow the manual, and damage in transit
  • Work not authorized by RSF in advance

The warranty isn't transferable, and RSF doesn't pay freight on replacement parts.

Not required on a non-combustible floor. Otherwise install the supplied guard (5" x 36" sheet metal) halfway under the fireplace and halfway under the hearth extension, centered on the door opening; it extends 2½" beneath the fireplace.

specGas.title: Gas log conversion
specGas.html:
Gas log setUp to 35,000 BTU, listed to ANSI Z21.60/CSA 2.26
Combustion air controlFully open whenever the gas log runs
BypassOpen at all times
Gas line entry1 ½" hole on each side, about 9" up from the bottom
ClearancesNone required by RSF; keep the gas log maker's

Vented sets only: the fireplace has not been tested with an unvented gas log set, and its heat permanently damages a gas log lighter (p. 6). Gas line by qualified personnel, to local code.

  1. Remove and keep the round central refractory brick, the two bottom bricks, and the firebox central plug (bolt, locknut, top and bottom plates). All go back if the unit returns to wood.
  2. On the gas side, remove the side firebrick, drill through the side of the firebox from outside, and drill or break a hole in the firebrick for the line.
  3. Leave the ash pan hole completely open; it brings air to the gas log.
  4. Install and run the log per its maker's instructions. The valve may sit inside the firebox if the log maker allows it and clearances are met.

conflicts.issue: Which way the air control lever opens: p. 9 says fully open is up ('all the way open (up)'); p. 4 says 'moved to the right as far as possible', p. 11 'all the way to the right in the open position', p. 28 'all the way open (towards the right)'. Shown in the air and light drawers.

Door position: p. 3 (Do's item 3) says to operate with the door fully closed because a partly open door can draw gas and flame out; the lighting (p. 11) and reloading (p. 12) procedures say to leave the door slightly open/ajar until the wood catches. Shown in the light and reload drawers.

Minimum catalyst temperature: p. 4 says smoke passing through the catalyst must be 'at least 150°C-300°F' or it soots up; p. 11 says the catalyst must be at least 175°C (350°F) to burn off smoke, and p. 12 says to keep the bypass open below 175°C (350°F).
conflicts.reason: Different quantities: p. 4 gives the temperature the smoke passing through the catalyst needs to keep soot off it (at least 150°C-300°F); pp. 11-12 give the temperature the catalyst itself needs before it burns off smoke, and the probe reading below which the bypass stays open (175°C (350°F)). Both hold together; the catalyst drawer now states each one.

review.notes: Single 34-page installation & operation manual; text is clean pdftotext with no French or offset-font scrambling. Manual text does not state firebox volume, max log length, overall dimensions or weight, glass/view area, heating area or mobile-home approval, so those catalog values could not be checked. Figure 1 (p. 7) is a dimension drawing: only its two labeled callouts were used (side standoff to side of opening 7 1/8"; base to top of opening 26 3/8"); an unlabeled 5/8" callout and the overall dimensions were not transcribed. Figure 6 framing examples (p. 17) are a dimensioned drawing with unlabeled numbers; not transcribed. Pages 30-31 (Complete Options List, including which options need electricity, referenced on p. 6) have no extractable text; the p. 32 Configured Options chart is a check-mark table, so required/optional/not-available status was not transcribed. Gravity-vent requirements come from the text on pp. 4-5 and 26. Replacement parts page (p. 33) only says parts 'will be available soon'. The manual names no safety listing standard for the fireplace; the certification line uses its stated EPA 2020 emission-standard compliance (p. 4). The listing label is on the bottom of the unit (p. 29) and is not reproduced. p. 9 says a combustible mantel 'cannot be wider than 12"'; the guide uses Table 1 (J) wording (max depth 12"). p. 26 says the supplied 5" x 36" spark guard 'can be cut to the minimum width' of Table 1 (I), which is also 36" - worth checking. Do's item 3 on p. 3 is garbled as printed ('with the door either fully closed'). Table 3: only the straight-chimney column is transcribed; offset columns are referenced. The manual prints Table 3 with curly foot/inch marks; the guide uses straight quotes. The 'pilot' on p. 12 is an air tube between the andiron posts, not a gas pilot. Warranty years are written as words in the manual (first year, second through fifth, sixth through thirtieth) and kept that way; the catalyst schedule is printed as 'first two (2) years', '3rd year 60%' etc. Owner drawers state the air lever as 'all the way to the right' only where p. 11 does, with the conflict note alongside.
